q: How do you say 'thank you' in Japanese?
explain: Arigatō is the normal 'thank you'; adding gozaimasu (arigatō gozaimasu) makes it more polite.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Thank you. (normal) ありがとう。 Arigatō. (ah-ree-GAH-toh)

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Thank you. (less formal) ありがとうございます。 Arigatō gozaimasu.

q: How do you say 'please' when making a request in Japanese?
explain: Onegai shimasu is 'please' for a request; for offering something, Japanese uses dōzo instead.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Please. (request) お願いします。 Onegai shimasu. (oh-neh-gah-ee shee-mahs)

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Please. (offer) どうぞ。 Dōzo. (Dohh-zoh)

q: How do you say the number 1 in Japanese?
explain: Ichi (一) is the standard reading of 1; the native counting form is hitotsu.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: 1 一 / 壱 ( ichi )

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: | 1 | 一 | ichi ( いち ) | hito(tsu) ( ひと・つ ) | ichi ( いち ) |

q: How do you say the number 3 in Japanese?
explain: San (三) is the standard reading of 3; the native counting form is mittsu.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: 3 三 / 参 ( san )

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: | 3 | 三 | san ( さん ) | mit(tsu) ( みっ・つ ) | san ( さん ) |

q: What is the usual way to say the number 4 in Japanese?
explain: 4 can be read yon or shi; yon is used in most situations, reportedly due to superstition because shi also means 'death'.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: 4 四 ( yon or shi )

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Note that, due to superstition ( shi also means "death"), the native Japanese readings yon and nana or 4 and 7 are used instead in most situations, though the Sino-Japanese readings shi and shichi respectively are more commonly used when counting.

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: As noted above, yon (4) and nana (7) are preferred to shi and shichi.

q: What is the usual way to say the number 7 in Japanese?
explain: 7 is read nana or shichi; nana is preferred in most situations, while shichi is common when counting.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: 7 七 ( nana or shichi )

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: | 7 | 七 | shichi ( しち ) | nana(tsu) ( なな・つ ) | nana ( なな ) |

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: As noted above, yon (4) and nana (7) are preferred to shi and shichi.

q: How do you say the number 9 in Japanese?
explain: Kyū (九) is the preferred reading of 9; ku is an alternative reading.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: 9 九 ( kyū )

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: | 9 | 九 | ku , kyū ( く, きゅう ) | kokono(tsu) ( ここの・つ ) | kyū ( きゅう ) |

q: How do you say the number 10 in Japanese?
explain: Jū (十) is the standard reading of 10; tens are built from it, e.g. ni-jū for 20.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: 10 十 / 拾 ( jū )

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: | 10 | 十 | jū ( じゅう ) | tō ( とお ) | jū ( じゅう ) |

sources.title: Japanese numerals - Wikipedia
sources.quote: Tens from 20 to 90 are "(digit) -jū " as in 二十 ( ni-jū ) to 九十 ( kyū-jū ) .

q: How do you say 'what?' in Japanese?
explain: Nani means 'what?'; it often becomes nan before desu, as in kore wa nan desu ka ('what is this?').

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: What? 何？ Nani? (nah-nee)

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: これは何ですか？ Kore wa nan desu ka? ("What [is] this?")

q: How do you say 'who?' in Japanese?
explain: Dare means 'who?', as in anata wa dare desu ka ('who are you?'). Do not confuse it with dore ('which?').

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Who? 誰？ Dare? (dah-reh)

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: あなたはだれですか？ Anata wa dare desu ka? ("Who [are] you?")

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: Which? どれ？ Dore? (doh-reh)

q: How do you say 'I don't understand' in Japanese?

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: I don't understand. 分かりません。 Wakarimasen. (wah-kah-ree-mah-sen)

q: What do you say when finishing a meal to thank the host or chef in Japanese?
explain: Gochisōsama deshita ('it was delicious') is said when finishing a meal; itadakimasu is said before starting one.

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: It was delicious. (when finishing a meal) ご馳走さまでした。 ( Gochisōsama deshita. )

sources.title: Japanese phrasebook – Travel guide at Wikivoyage
sources.quote: If your meal was good, thank the chef or staff with Gochisōsama deshita when leaving, and you'll get an extra-hearty thank you in return!
